newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIA PRODUCTS OUTLOOK - WEAKER AS WEST FALTERS.
newsitem.headline: ASIA PRODUCTS OUTLOOK - WEAKER AS WEST FALTERS.

text.p: Asia's oil products market which was supported most of last week by strong Western crude and product values, showed signs of cracking as Western prices faltered, traders said on Monday.
They said except for fuel oil, which is propped up by tight supplies and scattered demand, regional demand for middle and light distillates remains soft and stocks are high.
While a number of refiners in Singapore have cut their crude processing rates, traders noted that they have also been refining more lighter grades.
This in effect reduced fuel oil supplies, but middle and light distillate stocks are expected to continue to climb from the high levels seen last week, they said.
But despite the glum outlook on distillate prices, refiners are taking consolation from positive primary processing profit margins, estimated at around 50 cents per barrel on Friday.

For the week ended August 6, Singapore's Trade Development Board (TDB) reported that middle distillates stocks gained another 347,000 barrels to 11.047 million, while light distillates rose 53,000 million barrels to 7.081 million.
Residue stocks lost 688,000 barrels to 10.167 million.
Traders said current stocks are sufficient for any sudden spurt in winter demand for heating fuels jet-kerosene fuel and gas oil.
In addition, Singapore refiners are facing pressure from their South Korean counterparts who are offering gas oil aggressively, especially to China, which is fast becoming their niche market.
This was illustrated by the bulk of gas oil sales into China in June, amounting to more than 800,000 tonnes, which traders said came from South Korea as not much is being moved from Singapore.
But current poor Chinese demand has forced some Korean refiners to store their products in independent storage tanks in Subic Bay in the Philippines, traders said.

While Chinese buyers have emerged on the swaps market on Monday to limit a drastic price fall after Friday's 68-cent slide with a trade at $22.40 for late August lifting, this did not signal China's return to the physical market, traders said.
India was also expected to put a damper on the market in October, when the monsoon on the Indian east coast would limit its purchases to three or four cargoes.

India' last big purchase was in July when it took about 855,000 tonnes, but has since then brought little cheer to the market, limiting its August imports to 165,000 tonnes and 90,000 tonnes in September.
Some traders are pinning their hopes on a surge in demand from India in November and December, right through to March next year.

But India's recent purchase of larger term volumes from Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC) might also mean that its spot imports during the traditionally high demand period (November-March) might be lower than in previous years.

India took 2.07 million tonnes of 1.0-percent sulphur diesel from KPC in its new term contract at a 25-cent per barrel premium to MidEast quotes, free-on-board (fob) basis, up from 1.5 million tonnes in 1996-1997.
The price was lower than the 70-cent premium that India paid in the last contract.
In addition, India has also formalised its term purchase of 0.25-percent sulphur diesel from KPC, taking 1.08 million tonnes at a 92-cent premium, fob.
India paid less for its 1.08 million tonnes of kerosene in the new contract at a 22-cent premium, from 52 cents previously.

Indonesia's gas oil and kerosene demand in September was also not expected to be as large as in July and August, because the 200,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) crude unit at Balikpapan, which closed for maintenance on July 10, is being restarted.
Whatever additional demand Indonesia might have could be attributed to the shutdown of a smaller unit, the 100,000-bpd crude unit at Cilacap for 35 days from this week, traders said.

The gasoline market was mixed with the higher octane firmer due to cuts in reforming runs and high prices of the octane-booster methyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE), but lower octane prices are under pressure due to oversupply.
The overall sentiment is bearish as the western market, which has been strong due to the driving season, is now under pressure as demand softens.
The market is now seeking direction from Taiwan's import tender for at least two cargoes of 95-octane unleaded gasoline for September delivery, which would be awarded on Tuesday.
Traders said offers into this tender are expected to be lower than those made into an earlier tender which was cancelled.
High stocks of naphtha and low petrochemical prices in North Asia are weighing down on naphtha prices, traders said.
This would also dampen Abu Dhabi National Oil Co's (ADNOC) chances of getting consensus from term buyers on its offer for about 200,000 tonnes for September 1997-July 1998 liftings.
ADNOC offer stands at $22 per tonne over its formula, on an fob basis, compared to current term prices of $7.15.
Sentiment on the fuel oil market were more bullish as a Middle East trader emerged to support the market in the face of selling pressure from two major oil companies, traders said.
MidEast supplies are also slightly below normal due to better demand there.
Traders said firmer prices were also partly influenced by expectations of better bunker demand on news of the closure of South Korean ports as typhoon Tina approached the country's coast.
South Korean bunker sellers said they expect the ports to remain shut for two days until early Sunday.
